extracted.intended_audience: media/journalism scholars, journalism students and practitioners interested in newsworthiness/news values
extracted.subtask_description: A taxonomy and definitions of news values used to evaluate the newsworthiness of events, imagery and media content. Intended to guide content analysis, newsroom selection and academic study of what makes events 'news'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that there is a threshold the event will have to pass before it will be recorded at all (Galtung & Ruge’s term).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger, more violent or higher-profile events pass a visibility threshold and therefore have higher news value; small-scale events may not be recorded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size
rubrics_metrics.description: Size is the quantification or the 'largeness', 'weightiness', or 'frequency' of an occurrence or the number of people, animals, places, or things affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events need to be of a scale large enough to warrant attention; the more people involved the greater the newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superlativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that are the 'biggest', 'most violent', 'most destructive' etc. have greater news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage favors extremes (the biggest building, most violent crime) — superlative elements attract headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The measurable magnitude of an event (e.g., number of casualties, size of damage) contributes to newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantifiable magnitude enhances perceived importance and selection for coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale/Scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The geographical or social scale of an event — how widespread or far-reaching it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events that 'occur on a grand scale' or affect many people have higher news value; scale interacts with impact and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity/Discontinuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharp, temporally bounded events (sudden deviations from the norm) are easier to fit into news rhythms and thus more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slow processes (e.g., climate change) become newsworthy when they 'go critical' and can be condensed into a narrow event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative news (problems, scandals, conflict, crime, disaster) is generally preferred to positive news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative items satisfy frequency and consensus criteria, provide drama and shock value, and therefore attract audiences; 'bad news is good news.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Valence: Aggression
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of aggression (acts of violence, injuring or killing) increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include warlike incidents, murder, hostages — physical violence is highly newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valence: Controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with controversy or vehement dispute between parties attract attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political disputes, protests, strikes and clashing debates dramatize events and are selected for coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valence: Values
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that reference or threaten basic human values or civil rights are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items touching on core values increase audience interest and editorial selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Any form of conflict (physical, legal, intellectual, psychological) is newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict dramatizes stories and provides framing across diverse materials; 'if it bleeds it leads.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviance
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that deviate from norms (criminality, scandal, pathological or normative deviance) attract news attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deviance includes statistical oddity, normative breaches and sensational behaviour — all increase news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that produce dramatic structure (opposed viewpoints, tension, crisis) enhance newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drama often arises from conflict and negative valence; it helps hold audience attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad news
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories characterized as bad news — disaster, accident, crime, famine, war — are staple elements of news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such stories satisfy news selection criteria and are commonly prioritized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valence: Success
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive change, satisfactory completion, rescue or restoration are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although negativity dominates, positive outcomes (rescues, cures) also carry news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good news
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with particularly positive overtones (successes, happy outcomes) that attract audience attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be used to diversify bulletin tone; often appear as human-interest or feature pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Items that have considerable significance for large numbers in the audience — impact, consequence or social importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Importance explains inclusion beyond other criteria; large-scale social significance elevates newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance: Consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: The occurrence has consequences affecting many people or the audience (past or future significance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact is often synonymous with newsworthiness; stories affecting lives, finances or futures are prioritized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance: Concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that raise concern or are of immediate importance to audience welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories connected to personal experiences or living conditions increase perceived relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: General preference for information about events relevant to readers — cognitive and social constraint on selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevance may be personalized in reporting to help audiences relate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social significance
rubrics_metrics.description: A dimension combining importance/impact and interest, often correlated with deviance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social significance addresses how events affect society or communities and is used by journalists to judge news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum total of a story's parts, representing its weight and wider significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bigger the impact, the bigger the story; impact reflects both immediate and longer-term effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A measure of appeal to the audience; how much attention a story will attract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interest can be cognitive or emotional and is often used to personalize or humanize stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: How an event's outcomes affect the audience or society; its significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence is central to judging importance and whether a story merits coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recency
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement that news be up to date and refer to events as close to transmission time as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional competition for 'earliest intelligences' and the news media's production periodicity make recency crucial; 'the best news is something which has only just happened.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Relates to the 'when' of an event and whether the event is current, has a use-by date, or ties to anniversaries/trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness includes topicality and currency; assess whether new comment or circumstance adds to debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Material's relation to current debates or developments — how topical it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that connect to ongoing controversies or trends have currency and higher news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a story is about current issues or fits current public discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topical items are more likely to be included due to audience interest in current affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical, cultural or psychological nearness of an event to the audience or news outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local or culturally proximate events take precedence over distant ones; proximity may convert a national story into a local one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability of audiences to identify with the news — cultural familiarity or closeness in experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification can be geographic, cultural or ideological and helps make stories comprehensible and relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which an event is interpretable within the cultural framework of the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events loaded with meaning for readers (even if geographically distant) can be newsworthy due to implied relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Closeness in cultural terms which affects audience interest and interpretability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural proximity may operate alongside geographic proximity to determine relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnocentrism
rubrics_metrics.description: A tendency to favor events involving the in-group or culturally familiar actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethnocentric biases can influence which foreign stories are covered and how they are framed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondence to what we expect or want to happen; compatibility with socially-shared norms and mental scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that fit familiar 'news scripts' or preconceptions are more readily selected and shaped into coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotype
rubrics_metrics.description: The compatibility of a story with preconceptions about a social group or nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stereotypical events fit mental schemas and are easier to report and understand, boosting news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the consumer expects to be told about this event; predictability for the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expected occurrences (those that fit ongoing themes) may be privileged in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement that news be about new events; the newness or unusualness of an event increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty includes surprise, oddity and deviation from routine — the 'man-bites-dog' principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: The event is unlikely or surprising relative to expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected events attract attention; surprise often interacts with meaning and consonance to become news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviance (statistical/pathological/normative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degrees of deviance: statistical deviance (rarity), pathological deviance (threat to status quo), normative deviance (would violate norms if it occurred locally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different forms of deviance explain why unusual or norm-challenging events are newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Element of surprise or contrast that sets an event apart from ordinary occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise can be an independent driver of news selection (unexpectedness/novelty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarity/Oddity (Novelty/Rarity/Oddity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which an event is odd or rare in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oddity and rarity are attractive to audiences and increase selection probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unusualness
rubrics_metrics.description: Being out of the ordinary or not predicted; the exception rather than the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine events are less likely to be covered; unusual events are favoured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an event involves well-known persons, nations or organizations — 'big names' are better news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What a president or celebrity does carries more news value than similar actions by unknowns, unless other criteria (conflict, human interest) apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite-centred
rubrics_metrics.description: News centered on elites (powerful people, institutions, nations) because their actions are consequential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elites provide objects of identification and are more likely to be covered; includes powerful organizations and nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliteness
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of involving elite persons or institutions which elevates news salience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliteness often interacts with credibility and prominence in determining selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status: Elite nation
rubrics_metrics.description: International news involving high-status nations (e.g., permanent UN Security Council members) has greater news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events involving elite nations are prioritized in international coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status: Elite institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage preference for actions by major institutions (UN, NATO, top government bodies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional status contributes to perceived consequence and audience interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status: Elite person
rubrics_metrics.description: Prominence of individual persons (leaders, celebrities) increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public interest extends into private lives of public figures; elite persons often attract sustained coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning already-famous people have intrinsic news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Celebrity draws audience attention and can circularly generate further exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power
rubrics_metrics.description: Involvement of people or organizations with power (political, economic) heightens newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powerful actors' actions are more consequential and thus more likely to be covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing complex processes or institutions to the actions of individuals to make stories comprehensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personification emphasizes people at the center of events and aids dramatization and identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency to focus on individuals and personal examples rather than abstract processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalization helps audiences relate and remember stories; people are easier to photograph and narrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification: Emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Using emotional, touching aspects to create audience identification and empathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotive framing increases engagement and can convert issues into human stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Using familiar people, settings or tropes to make material more accessible to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiar elements aid comprehension and retention of news items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that tug at emotions, offer human faces, entertain or inspire empathy; often feature animals, children, heroes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human interest is broad (humorous to tragic) and often linked to novelty and entertainment; commonly associated with feature/soft stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Material chosen for its captivating, amusing or diverting quality to attract large audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News programmes account for entertainment value; material may be selected for humour, titillation or spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories framed to arouse strong emotions or shock; short, dramatic occurrences that can be sensationalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensationalism emphasizes emotion-arousing aspects and dramatic presentation to increase attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for items that have a clear, limited number of meanings; less ambiguity increases noticeability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous events are less favoured; clarity of interpretation helps selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency to simplify content to make reports more easily understandable for audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists reduce complexity, summarise background and make stories suitable for the production format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should be closely packed with facts and little padding; concise presentation is preferred, especially in broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brevity concerns both time and space; editing to fit allotted slots is a core news-writing objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presupposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumption about prior information; necessary background may need summarisation for audiences unfamiliar with context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists must avoid assuming too much prior knowledge; provide enough context for comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensuring stories clarify confused matters and contain enough explicit reference to be understood standalone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearcut stories with impeccable sources are favoured; clarity reduces interpretive ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of vivid detail or anecdote to enliven stories and aid engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colour enhances readability and memorability; often used in feature writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall assessment of action, pace, completeness, clarity and technical/aesthetic features of the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality storytelling (pace, completeness) increases likelihood of selection and audience satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a story satisfies audience informational needs and leaves few unanswered questions (opposite of suspense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that provide required closure and information are favored in some formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire to present a 'balanced' whole — a mixture and packaging of different kinds of news within a bulletin or outlet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors seek variety by subject, geography and demography; how a news item fits surrounding items matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-option
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting tangential items in terms of a high-profile continuing story to fit agenda or package.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items may be reinterpreted to fit dominant narratives or continuing themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining balance within a programme or bulletin (e.g., domestic vs international, hard vs soft news).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement and mix of items are considered to offer a balanced programme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition/Fit
rubrics_metrics.description: How an item fits with others that surround it and the overall editorial package.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fit can determine whether an item is included or omitted based on slot characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: The time-span needed for an event to unfold relative to the medium's production frequency — events matching the medium's cycle are more likely recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events with frequencies aligned to daily/weekly production cycles are advantaged; frequency also drives 'scoops' and ongoing coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an item has hit the headlines it tends to stay there; ongoing themes facilitate follow-up coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity encourages sustained coverage; news items already on the agenda attract more related stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: The propensity to continue covering a story over time once it has been established as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors favor stories that produce subsequent developments or that can be updated frequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: News agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that set or fit the news organisation’s own editorial agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agenda-setting influences selection independent of other intrinsic event qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: The news barrier
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria (simplicity, identification, excitement) that allow items to pass through to coverage; once passed, similar reports follow more easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage through the 'news barrier' is aided by prepackaged text, prescheduled events, and compatibility with current themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that are expected in advance or known beforehand may be privileged (e.g., prescheduled events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictability interacts with the news cycle and production needs (easier to schedule and prepare coverage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence of ready-made text or material journalists can rapidly process into stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readily available copy increases the likelihood of coverage under time pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial and inter-outlet competition drives desire for exclusives and influences story choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competition for scoops and audience share shapes editorial priorities and resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organisational requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal organisational structures, budgets and mandates that constrain story choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements such as slot length, staffing and editorial policies affect which items are covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: External influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressures external to editorial judgement (proprietors, advertisers, political actors) that may shape content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns about independence and corruption of content are relevant to assessing news purity and selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facticity
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which a story contains facts and figures (locations, names, sums) on which 'hard news' thrives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard facts increase credibility and newsworthiness, especially for policy or investigative items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that leave audiences wondering what will happen next or that generate uncertainty over outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspense can be used to retain audience interest over time (serial coverage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Information kept secret by an actor (government, company, individual) that, when revealed, is newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure or revelation of secret information commonly increases selection and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty (Dynamics: Uncertainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events whose courses or consequences are unclear and unpredictable, generating news interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uncertainty can drive ongoing coverage as audiences seek resolution; related to suspense and follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual attractiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual qualities of imagery that make a story includable because of film availability or dramatic visual qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If compelling film or photography is available (dramatic shots), that alone may justify coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of a photographic or filmable moment that enhances an event's newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Picture opportunities are especially valuable for television and online visual platforms and can influence selection.
